title: PI-FD: Property Inference Attacks on Federated Learning With Distillation via Synthetic Data Generation
summary: Shows that federated learning with distillation, in which clients upload only logits computed on a shared public dataset, still leaks population-level properties of their private data. The attack, PI-FD, has the malicious server synthesise a private-domain dataset from the observed victim logits, train shadow models on it, and read demographic or prevalence properties off their behaviour. CTGAN is run as a substitute for the paper's own generator in an ablation that asks whether an off-the-shelf tabular synthesiser would do: attack accuracy falls to chance in every case, which is the result the paper uses to argue its logit-conditioned synthesis is what makes the attack work.
evidence: section VII.D, Comparisons With Existing Generative Approaches, states that replacing the paper's private domain synthesis with representative tabular generators, specifically CTGAN and TabSyn, causes attack accuracy to drop to 50.00% across all evaluated cases, equivalent to random guessing; Table 13 reports the comparison

title: Differentially Private Synthetic Adversarial Network Traffic Generation Based on Tabular Diffusion Processes
summary: Proposes DP-NetDDPM, which applies a tabular denoising diffusion model to adversarial network packet generation under differential privacy, on the argument that diffusion captures packet-format structure and distribution better than the GAN and autoencoder synthesisers previously used for intrusion-detection data. TVAE, released alongside CTGAN, is one of the three synthesisers it is measured against on t-SNE distribution alignment, fidelity and machine-learning adaptability; CTGAN itself is named in the related-work account of GAN approaches to mixed types and imbalance but is not among the models run.
evidence: the baselines section describes TVAE as a VAE model designed for tabular data using Gumbel-Softmax for categorical and numerical features and retains it for its public availability; Figure 3 compares TVAE against real data on 2D and 3D t-SNE; the results section reports the proposed model outperforming TVAE and CTABGAN on ML adaptability; CTGAN appears only in the related-work paragraph on GAN-based approaches

title: A Comparative Study of GAN-Based Methods for Tabular Synthetic Data Generation
summary: Implements CTGAN, CTAB-GAN and ADS-GAN on the Adult, Credit Card and Wine Quality datasets and compares the synthetic tables they produce through histograms and correlation heatmaps, Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Chi-Square tests, the TabSynDex composite metric, and downstream machine-learning efficacy, concluding that no model dominates: ADS-GAN holds statistical fidelity and correlation best, CTGAN handles complex multimodal distributions best, and CTAB-GAN is the most consistent. The study is framed explicitly as supplying the broad comparison the CTGAN paper did not attempt, and CTGAN is one of the three models it trains and evaluates.
evidence: the abstract states that the methods used include implementation of three GAN models, CTGAN, CTAB-GAN and ADS-GAN, on Adult, Credit Card and Wine Quality; the introduction states that previous research introduced CTGAN and demonstrated its effectiveness but focused solely on establishing its capabilities without comparing it against other models, which is the gap this study addresses; section II credits CTGAN with mode-specific normalization for continuous variables and conditional vectors for categorical ones

title: Benchmarking Generative Adversarial Networks for Realistic Tabular Data Generation
summary: Compares three GAN architectures for privacy-preserving tabular synthesis on the Medical Cost Personal dataset under identical preprocessing and training, scoring them on statistical, distributional and diversity metrics to see which best preserves the original structure. CTGAN and TGAN are two of the three models trained and evaluated, with CTGAN credited for mode-specific normalization of continuous fields and conditional generation over categorical ones, and TGAN for fitting entries sequentially to hold column dependencies.
affiliations: SRM Institute of Science and Technology
KPR Institute of Engineering and Technology
Sri Ramakrishna Institute of Paramedical Sciences
PSG INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND APPLIED RESEARCH
evidence: the abstract states that three GAN-based models, CTGAN, TGAN and CapsuleGAN, are employed in the experimental comparison using the Medical Cost Personal Dataset; the related-work section names CTGAN by Xu et al. as one of the earliest and strongest tabular-specific architectures for its mode-specific normalization and conditional generation; the experimental setup section confirms all three were trained under the same preprocessing and training procedures

title: Ensemble-based Synthetic Data Synthesis for Federated QoE Modeling
summary: Addresses the problem that quality-of-experience models need labelled data pooled across subjects while data-protection regulation blocks sharing the local datasets, and proposes synthesising shareable substitutes with an ensemble of Bayesian network models trained at each site. CTGAN is the tabular-GAN prior art the design departs from: the paper credits it with addressing multi-modality and varying distribution in continuous attributes through conditional GANs and preprocessing, then declines to adopt it, judging the per-dataset manual work and the tuning burden across its component algorithms too heavy for the QoE datasets in hand.
evidence: the related-work discussion states that challenges including multi-modality and varying distribution in continuous attributes are addressed with indicative results using conditional GANs and preprocessing techniques, and that these are hard to replicate on the paper's datasets because of the extra manual work per dataset and the complexity of tuning the plurality of algorithms involved; the paper favours a Bayesian ensemble instead. Xplore reports the reference list as unavailable for this document, so the citation is identified from the prose description of CTGAN's two contributions rather than from the bibliography entry

title: Is Synthetic Flow Data from Generative Models Ready for Network Intrusion Detection Systems?
summary: Builds one evaluation pipeline for synthetic network-flow data and puts a representative of each generative family through it — a GAN, a diffusion model and a language model — measuring not only distributional similarity but the downstream intrusion-detection performance that follows from training on the generated flows, with attention to minority attack classes. CTGAN is the GAN-family representative: it gets its own methodology subsection describing the conditional generator and training strategy that address mode collapse and imbalanced categoricals, its training and sampling workflow is diagrammed, and it is trained and sampled on the benchmark flows.
evidence: section I states the unified evaluation pipeline assesses three generative models, CTGAN from the GAN family, TabDDPM from the diffusion family and GReaT from the LLM family; section III.B, Overview of CTGAN, describes its two components and Figure 2 illustrates the workflow for training CTGAN and generating synthetic data; section II notes prior studies used CTGAN to generate minority-class instances for NIDS datasets without addressing generated-data quality
